prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, which brought atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level and opened new tests of fundamental physics

statement.case_for: After reading all eight opening ballots I move my own preference from circuit QED to the optical lattice clock. Seven of eight members ranked it, four placed it in their top three and two placed it first, and the reasons given are scientific rather than merely popular. The magic-wavelength idea removed the old trade-off between atom number and motional and light shifts, and the JILA strontium work then showed that thousands of atoms interrogated together can reach about 1e-18 fractional uncertainty. That is a new regime of precision, not an incremental refinement. It is reproduced and intercompared across RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA/NIST, PTB, SYRTE and NPL, which answers my usual question about robustness across laboratories. The physics payoff is already realised: relativistic redshift resolved over millimetres, bounds on drifting constants, and the pending redefinition of the second. The credited pair, Katori for the proposal and first demonstration and Ye for the record accuracy and many-body regime, is a clean two-person attribution, which is rare and valuable. I also hold that the discovery, not the application, is what we reward, and here the discovery is clearly one of measurement physics.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is the overlap with prizes already given: the 2005 prize covered the frequency comb that makes optical clocks countable and the 2012 prize covered single-ion control and ion clocks, so the committee could regard the lattice clock as a refinement of recognised work. Credit is also incomplete, since ion-clock groups (aluminium-ion clocks), Lemonde, Takamoto and Kimble's group on the magic-wavelength and early lattice experiments lie outside the credited names. A second reservation is that the SI second has not yet been redefined, so one could argue the cleanest narrative moment lies a few years ahead, although the science does not depend on that decision.

responses.point: Mehlig ranked optical lattice clocks last of his eight and raised the worry that the field may be judged an incremental extension of the frequency-comb and ion-clock prizes, while also noting that the magic-wavelength credit may extend beyond Katori and Ye.
responses.response: I take the overlap concern seriously but think it is answered by what is new. The comb is a ruler and the ion clock is a single-particle reference; the lattice clock is a different physical idea, a state-insensitive trap that lets thousands of atoms be probed at once, and it brought a statistical advantage of orders of magnitude. That is why it accessed new regimes such as millimetre-scale gravitational redshift and spin-exchange physics in a many-body clock. On the priority point I agree the early history is shared, but the proposal and first realisation are Katori's and the record accuracy is Ye's, so the two-name credit survives scrutiny better than most of what is on our list.

responses.point: Eriksson placed lattice clocks sixth, arguing that they are clean and lasting but that the ion-clock contribution (for example Al+) is not credited and the redefinition of the second is still pending.
responses.response: I agree the redefinition is pending and that Al+ and other ion clocks are an uncredited parallel line. I would not delay for the redefinition, because that is a metrological decision and the physics is secure and cross-checked among laboratories today. I also disagree mildly with the implicit comparison with twisted bilayer graphene: I rank that case highly too, but its superconducting mechanism is still debated, while the clock has no comparable open question about whether the result is real. If Eriksson thinks a different two-person split would be fairer, I would like to hear which names.

responses.point: Danielsson ranked IceCube first and topological insulators second, valuing discoveries found in nature and flagging that large-collaboration credit and the origin of the diffuse flux are unsettled.
responses.response: I defer to Danielsson and Pearce on neutrino astronomy, as astroparticle physics is outside my expertise. My only qualification is attribution: Danielsson himself notes that decisive credit may sit outside the three names, and Halzen, Karle and Spiering as a trio is harder to defend than a pair whose individual contributions are documented in two separate papers. A clock is also an instrument-based discovery in his own sense, since it measures something nature does, namely time dilation, and I regard the two as comparable in kind. I would not stand in the way of B061 if the committee found its three-name credit defensible.

responses.point: Pearce ranked IceCube first and lattice clocks second, noting the precision and systematics work behind clocks and that the frequency-comb and ion-trap prizes could make the committee cautious.
responses.response: We agree on the science and on the main caution. Where I differ is on ordering: both are mature, but only the clock case has a two-person credit that all seven ranking members endorsed, and the same Katori and Ye pair was proposed by everyone who ranked it. That consistency counts for something when the three-laureate limit is a real constraint, as it is for IceCube. I would like the committee to treat the IceCube and clock cases as genuine competitors, and I would support a different outcome if the expert report shows that the IceCube credit can be stated more cleanly than I currently believe.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, or sees them as a successor to them.
Whether early magic-wavelength and lattice-clock priority (Lemonde, Takamoto, Kimble and others) is adequately covered by the two credited names.
How much weight the committee should give to the pending redefinition of the second when judging timing.
I am outside my own field for IceCube, topological insulators and twisted bilayer graphene, so my ordering among those cases is provisional and I would defer to colleagues.
statement.conflict_note: I am director of the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and a close colleague of the superconducting-circuit community, so I should be recused or at least discount my view on B041 (circuit QED), which I ranked first at opening; for that reason I do not make it my preferred configuration and list it only as an alternative. Chalmers MC2 has hosted laureates and guest researchers in circuit physics, which is another reason to treat B041 with caution. I have no specific personal or institutional connection to Katori, Ye or their laboratories apparent from my profile.
